name: Mirror flip / symmetry test

lead: The mirror flip test compares a face photo with its left-right reversed copy, or builds composites from each half of the face, to see how symmetrical it looks. It is a common self-check in facial-analysis content.

The chain: flip or split the photo, judge left-right differences, then target asymmetries or choose angles. Research treats symmetry as one of three factors, with averageness and youthfulness, in attractiveness judgments; studies from the 1990s and 2000s found symmetrical faces tend to be rated as more attractive, with a larger effect for female faces. No published study has evaluated the test itself.

paras: People reverse a photo horizontally or build left-left and right-right composites in a photo app and compare them with the original, looking at eyes, brows, jaw and nose. Results are used to choose which side to show or what to address with grooming, hair or procedures.

Researchers note mirrored composites can create artificial features, and natural expression adds temporary asymmetry. Press coverage has linked appearance-rating practices to body dysmorphia concerns.

angle.text: Users reverse a face photo or compare its two halves to assess symmetry, one of several features in facial analysis, then target asymmetries or choose angles. Symmetry features in attractiveness research; this self-test itself has not been validated.

lead: The mirror flip or symmetry test is a self-assessment practice in which a person compares a photograph of their face with its left-right reversed copy, or compares the two halves of the face, to judge how symmetrical it looks. It belongs to the facial-analysis side of looksmaxxing, where symmetry is one of several features people assess.

Published research treats facial symmetry as one of three factors, with averageness and youthfulness, that influence judgments of attractiveness. Studies reported in the 1990s and 2000s found that more symmetrical faces tend to be rated as more attractive, with a larger effect for female faces.[1]

Researchers have also noted that creating symmetric composites by mirroring one half of a face can introduce artificial features, so conclusions drawn from mirrored images have been questioned.[1] No published study has evaluated the mirror flip test as a self-assessment method.
infobox: Compare a face photo with its mirror-reversed copy or half-face composites

paras: In the practice, a person views a flipped version of a photograph or builds composite images from each half of the face, then looks for differences between the original and reversed views. Facial-analysis discussions within looksmaxxing, which also rate features such as eye shape, cheeks and jawline, are described in coverage of the movement.[2]

Two kinds of asymmetry are discussed in the research literature. Fluctuating asymmetry refers to random left-right differences, while directional asymmetry is systematic; on average the eyes, nose and mouth sit slightly left of the axis through the ears, a difference that shrinks from about 2 degrees at birth to about 0.5 degrees in adults.[1]

Studies by Grammer and Thornhill (1994) and Rhodes and colleagues (1998) linked symmetry with attractiveness ratings, and Jones and colleagues (2001, 2004) found symmetric faces were judged healthier.[1] Some authors have proposed that symmetry signals 'good genes', a hypothesis described on the same page.[1]

Face-half mirroring has been used in experiments, but critics note it creates artificial features; for example, mirroring a slightly bent nose can produce an oversized or undersized nose.[1] Natural expression also adds temporary asymmetry; about 76% of people show greater mouth movement on the right side during speech.[1]
